title: Every Friday
hookLine: every Friday is a small day of penance, meat or another sacrifice by local rule

cards: Why does a fast-food chain well-known for burgers sell a fish sandwich?
The story told in the business world is that a franchise owner in a Catholic neighborhood was losing money every Friday because his customers wouldn't eat meat that day.
So he came up with a fish sandwich, and it went national. Whatever the details, the custom behind the story is real: Catholics going without meat on Fridays.
And the reason sits under every week of the year, not just Lent.

teach.b: The word is abstinence, from the Latin abstinere, to hold back. In Church law it means one thing: not eating meat. Fasting is different; it means eating less, one full meal.
Catholics fast and abstain on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and abstain on the Fridays of Lent. But canon law goes further.

teach.h: EVERY FRIDAY A DAY OF PENANCE.
teach.b: Every Friday of the year is a day of penance, kept in memory of the day Jesus died: a small Good Friday.
The law names abstinence from meat as the usual way to keep it, from age fourteen, unless a solemnity falls on that Friday, and it lets each country's bishops set the details.
That's where it gets local. In the United States since 1966, outside of Lent, the bishops allow Catholics to choose another penance instead: an act of charity, extra prayer, giving up something else.

In England and Wales, the bishops brought back the meat rule in 2011. So a Catholic in London and one in Chicago may keep Friday differently, and both are keeping the law. Why meat and not, say, bread?
One common explanation is that meat was the feast-day food, the one people looked forward to. Either way, the point was never that meat is bad.

teach.h: A SMALL NO FOR A LARGER YES.
teach.b: It's a small, regular no that makes room for a larger yes.

teach.h: LET HIM DENY HIMSELF, AND TAKE UP HIS CROSS DAILY.
teach.b: Jesus put it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily."

how: Catholic canon law makes every Friday a day of penance; many Catholics abstain from meat on all Fridays, and where bishops permit, as in the United States outside Lent, others choose a different penance such as charity or prayer.

games.q: you're a Catholic in Chicago on an ordinary Friday in July. what does the law ask of you?
o: some penance: no meat, or another sacrifice you choose.
games.why: every Friday is a day of penance. in the US outside Lent you may substitute another penance for meat, but not skip it.

practice: Think about your ordinary Friday and one small thing you could quietly go without, or add: meat is the classic, but it could be your phone at lunch, dessert, a drive you could walk, or an hour given to someone else.
Keep it small enough to keep. If you pray, offer it for someone; if you don't, notice how holding back feels.

wordCard.voice: Abstinence. From the Latin for holding back: in Church law, going without meat, the usual Friday penance, with local rules about substitutes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: every friday a little lent. A small no, every week, for a larger yes. That's day six hundred ninety.
